body:
Chapter 1
Jaliyah
"Just give me two minutes. Please," Jaliyah begged the future Alpha of her pack—Alpha Zephyra of the Moonhowl Tribe. Her hand rested on his arm, but he stared down at it with a frown before lifting his eyes—those deep, dark blue eyes she used to lose herself in—and shot her a cold, disapproving glare.
They’d been lovers for a little over a year, nothing serious by his standards. But now it was over. He had found his Fated Mate, handpicked by the Moon Goddess herself, and just like that, Jaliyah wasn’t even worth a minute of his time.
She had fallen for him completely, even though she’d always known this day would come. She’d kept things light, playful, never letting him see how deep her feelings ran. He wasn’t her fated mate, and she wasn’t his. All she wanted now was to wish him well and let him know she was leaving—going back to campus to finish her law degree full-time, interning during breaks. She wouldn’t be home for at least the next two years.
She couldn’t stand the thought of watching him be happy with someone else, seeing them all over each other like she and Zephyra used to be. Watching that would destroy her. But she’d never tell him that.
As she stood there, clutching his arm and trying to force a bright smile, Soraya—his mate—walked into the room. Her eyes locked onto Jaliyah’s hand on Zephyra, and her expression turned venomous. She didn’t care that Jaliyah and Zephyra had been childhood friends for twenty years, didn’t care about the bond they had once shared.
Soraya’s wolf growled deep in her chest, and then Soraya snapped, “Get your filthy hands off my mate,” as she stormed across the room. She grabbed Jaliyah’s wrist, yanking her away from Zephyra, and with her other hand, slapped her so hard across the face that Jaliyah staggered back a step, her hand flying to her burning cheek.
Ashira, Jaliyah’s wolf, howled with fury in her mind, enraged by the attack. Before Jaliyah could stop her, Ashira surged forward, claws extending from her fingertips as she retaliated with a fierce strike of her own. Her claws raked across Soraya’s cheek, leaving three deep, bloody scratches that dripped onto her clothes.
Soraya screamed in pain, her hands flying to her face as blood poured down. Tears streamed from her eyes as she turned to her mate, seeking comfort in his arms. Jaliyah knew she’d heal—wolves always did—but it didn’t matter. The damage was done.
Zephyra’s eyes widened in shock. He pulled Soraya into his arms, holding her close, protective. Then his gaze landed on Jaliyah, blazing with fury—his wolf clearly right there with him. His roar echoed through the room.
“Get out of this pack. Don’t ever come back.”
Jaliyah froze, heart pounding, tears welling in her green eyes. She knew what it meant. Attacking the Luna—or even the future Luna—was treason. Her wolf had drawn blood. That could mean exile… or worse. She turned and fled the room, knowing if she stayed even a second longer, the consequences could be deadly.
Ashira whimpered in anguish, devastated at the thought of leaving him, their home, their family. Both of them knew—they’d never be allowed back. If Zephyra were already Alpha, he might have marked her as a rogue on the spot, stripped her of her title, and thrown her out with nothing.
Jaliyah’s pace quickened as she rushed through the front door of the packhouse. Then she was running, tears streaming down her face, sprinting toward her car. She couldn’t wait. What if Zephyra—or worse, Soraya—changed their mind and decided banishment wasn’t enough? What if they wanted her punished more severely? Beaten? Locked up? Killed?
There was no time to say goodbye. Not to her mom, her dad, or her older brother. She just ran, climbed into her car, and peeled out of the driveway as fast as she could, desperate to get off pack land before anything else happened.
She heard a voice behind her—Darian, the future Beta—calling after her. “Jaliyah, what’s going on?” There was real concern in his voice, but she didn’t stop to explain. She couldn’t.
She just drove.
At least Zephyra didn’t have the authority to officially brand her a rogue. Yet. That decision would fall to his father, Alpha Thaddeus. He’d hear their side of the story—Zephyra’s and Soraya’s—and decide her fate.
‘Why?’ Jaliyah sobbed, asking Ashira as she sped down the road, heading back to the university where she’d been studying for the past two years. Thankfully, she had a dorm waiting for her. A roof. A place to hide. She could never go back to her pack.
‘Protect pup,’ Ashira whimpered in grief.
Jaliyah’s crying intensified. Her chest ached so badly she didn’t know if she could survive it. A baby. His baby. And he’d tossed her aside like trash without even knowing. Banished her. Cut her out of his life.
She had to survive—for the pup growing inside her. Even if it shattered her. Even if it tore her and Ashira apart.

Chapter 2
She stared at the letter in her hand, shaking so hard she could barely hold it steady. It had been six long years since she’d escaped the Moonhowl Tribe—and now here it was. An envelope sealed with her old pack’s crest. His crest.
Jaliyah lifted her gaze from the letter to the beautiful boy playing with his sisters on the living room floor. This couldn’t be happening. It just couldn’t.
Somehow, they’d made it. They’d survived. Built a life far away from the pack, safe and at peace. She had never gone back—not once. Just like he told her not to. And yet, she was still technically part of the Moonhowl Tribe. By some mercy of the Goddess, Alpha Thaddeus had never officially cut her off from the pack. There was still a faint bond tying her to it.
Her three kids were roughhousing, laughing, tumbling all over each other. Jaliyah had just come home from her job at Veritas Legal, a law firm in the human world—about as far from wolf society as one could get. Even when she had desperately needed support, she’d kept her distance. She’d learned how to survive on her own, how to be strong for her children. She’d built friendships with humans, created a kind of surrogate, human family to help ease the ache of isolation.
Her son—handsome, strong-willed, with a fire in his eyes—was so much like his father. With tousled blond hair and sun-kissed skin, he radiated life and energy. He looked up at her with vivid green eyes—her eyes. The only feature he inherited from her. Everything else, down to the stubborn chin and intense presence, came from his father. A man who loathed her.
The girls shared the same green eyes and blond hair, though theirs was long and wavy, softer in texture and temperament. Unlike Kael. Though he was only three minutes older than his identical twin sisters, Zaya and Mira, Kael was taller by two inches and always acted like their protector. People often assumed he was a year older than them. Jaliyah never corrected them.
She stepped into the kitchen, leaving the kids to play. Her eyes dropped back to the envelope. Even Ashira, her wolf, was silent in the back of her mind. Cautious. Uneasy. Jaliyah could feel the tension radiating from her, seeping into her own nerves.
She tore open the envelope and read the letter:
*****
Jaliyah Vale,
You are hereby summoned to return to the Moonhowl Tribe.
You must respond within seven days and provide a date for your return.
Alpha Zephyra – Moonhowl Tribe
*****
How he found her, she didn’t know. But she wasn’t going back.
Striking a match, she lit the gas stove and set the letter and envelope on fire. She watched as the flames consumed them, burning them down to ash. Defying him wasn’t something she should do—but she couldn’t go back. Not ever.
She grabbed her phone and started searching for new apartments. She needed to move—fast.
It took four days to find a place that was available immediately. It wasn’t close to her office, which meant she’d have to commute, but that didn’t matter. Jaliyah broke her lease, paid the penalty, and moved out with the kids as quickly as she could. She left behind their beautiful beachfront apartment for a larger one deeper in the city. The rent was the same, but the new place had more space for the kids to play—and more importantly, it had a doorman and overnight security. At least now, she wouldn’t be caught off guard.
She changed the kids’ school, too. She had never exactly hidden her identity—just stayed far enough away to be forgotten. Even Ashira had suffered because of it. She was rarely allowed to run free. Life in the human world was a constant strain, a daily punishment for one small crime.
One mistake to protect her unborn pups—and they’d all paid the price. That pain had made both her and Ashira stronger, more guarded. They didn’t follow their hearts anymore. Only logic. Only reality. No wolves were allowed in their world now. Not anymore.
Veritas Legal had become their home since she passed the Bar Exam. Peyton and Avery were her most trusted friends—humans who had no idea what she really was. Peyton had even delivered her babies, right in Avery’s office during what should’ve been a routine lunch meeting. Avery’s wife had been visiting that day, and thank the Goddess Peyton was a doctor.
All three children had been born there on the university campus. She remembered crying after they arrived, scared out of her mind and completely alone. She told Avery and Peyton the truth—or at least part of it: no family, no help, and the father didn’t care. That much was real. They took pity on her, this terrified 20-year-old with triplets and no support system.
Over time, they’d become like family to her. A second mom and dad—not that she ever called them that. But the bond was there, unspoken and solid.
No one knew who she really was. No one knew who the father of her kids was. It was a secret she’d take to the grave. Humans had no idea about wolfen society—by law, she wasn’t even allowed to tell them. Not that she ever would.
Ten days after she moved, another letter showed up at her new address.
A chill ran down her spine. Moving hadn’t worked.
She marked the envelope “Not at this address” and returned it, praying to the Goddess that this would be the end of it.
Two weeks later, another letter arrived. Again, she returned it unopened with the same message. In the human world, that would’ve been enough. It meant the person they were looking for didn’t live there.
She prayed again. Begged the Goddess to make it stop.
Because she couldn't go back.
She would never go back.
He had made sure of that.

Chapter 3
Zephyra
He held the second official letter in his hand—the one that had come back undelivered, just like the first. Well, almost like the first. That first one hadn’t come back, and he was sure she’d opened it. Curiosity would’ve gotten the better of her, if not a sense of duty to respond to her Alpha.
Zephyra knew they hadn’t ended things on good terms, but it was time for Jaliyah to come home. He’d caught a glimpse of her on TV completely by chance, standing on the courthouse steps, talking to the press about a case she’d just won—some high-profile divorce case she was handling.
Six years. It had been six damn years, and she looked incredible. Confident. Powerful. Radiating that sharp, no-nonsense energy. She was dressed to impress in a dark blue pencil skirt that hugged every curve down to her knees and a soft, cream-colored blouse that clung to her body in the breeze. Her bright green eyes were filled with life. She didn’t feed the media any drama, just gave them the facts and walked away.
Life outside the pack seemed to suit her. And that hurt a little more than he’d expected. Knowing he was the reason she was out there—alone—made something in his chest ache.
He and Ember, his wolf, had watched her closely. She’d always dreamed of being a lawyer. Sure, there wasn’t much demand for divorce attorneys within pack society, but contract law? That was another story. He remembered her saying that was what she wanted to specialize in back when she was still studying. They’d all been in the lounge that night—Zephyra, his Beta Darian, Gamma Talon, and Delta Maddox—winding down after a long day with a few drinks and flipping through channels when her face suddenly appeared on screen.
It was a recap of the day’s news from the human world. Her name and law firm scrolled across the bottom of the screen. Darian had the remote. They all froze when she came on. No one had seen her since that day—the day Zephyra had forced her to leave. She had obeyed, left, and never looked back. Just like he’d told her to.
Watching her now, so grown, so stunning at 26, hearing her voice again—it stirred something in him. Regret. He missed her. They’d grown up side by side, trained together, even been lovers once. But now she was just…gone.
‘Bring her home,’ Ember had growled, and he hadn’t stopped. Days passed, and the wolf kept pushing. Wouldn't let up. Eventually Zephyra caved. He agreed with his wolf—it was time. Time to bring her back where she belonged. So he sent that first official letter after Darian had tracked her down. It hadn’t even taken a full day. She wasn’t hiding—just keeping her distance.
Now, over a month later, he sat in his office, frustrated and just about ready to snap. She’d ignored that first letter—or maybe she hadn’t even received it. But he doubted that. Darian didn’t screw up, not with something like this. They’d all grown up together. Jaliyah had been just as close to Darian as she had been to him.
Darian had been furious the day she left—furious that Zephyra had made her go.
That day... Zephyra had been pissed, and so had Ember. They’d acted on instinct, pure emotion, no thought. He hadn’t really thought much about it since—until he saw her again.
Soraya had lost it when Jaliyah wasn’t stripped of her rank and cast out as a rogue by his father, Alpha Thaddeus. She’d demanded it, called it an insult. But his father had shut it down with a simple, “No. It’s inappropriate under the circumstances.” He’d known about Jaliyah and Zephyra’s relationship—that they’d been sleeping together for over a year—and he suspected Soraya had overreacted out of jealousy or spite.
Given Jaliyah’s recent move, the letter should’ve reached her. Maybe she didn’t get it. Or maybe she read it—and decided to run.
Zephyra turned the envelope over in his hand, then looked over at Darian. “So this is how she’s going to play it, huh?”
“You did tell her to leave and never come back,” Darian said flatly. He was leaning against the wall, arms crossed, looking bored. “If she didn’t get the first one and returned these last two, maybe she really doesn’t know what was inside.”
Zephyra stared at the envelope for a while, thinking. Then he gave a slow nod. “Fine. Let’s make it official—something she can’t ignore without us showing up to get her.”
Darian let out a sigh, his gray eyes narrowing. “You sure about that, boss? You really want to go that route?”
“Yes,” Zephyra said, his tone leaving no room for argument. “Send it to her law firm. Make sure it has to be signed for. That way, we’ll know she got it.”
A smug smile tugged at his lips.
‘Let’s see you ignore me now, Little Wolf,’ he thought. ‘I can play this game just as well as you can. The difference is, you don’t get to ignore me. I’m your Alpha. You will do as I command.’

Chapter 4
Jaliyah
Graham Sterling, CEO of Veritas Legal, stood in front of her desk, tapping a sleek black envelope against his palm while waiting patiently for her to finish her call. He didn’t interrupt—he knew she was speaking with a client.
As soon as she hung up, he said, “How do you know the Wolfe Corporation? And why haven’t you brought them in as a client?” His tone carried a hint of irritation, clearly annoyed she hadn’t mentioned her connection to such a major company.
But the second he uttered the words Wolfe Corporation, all she could feel was her heart slamming against her ribcage. Her gaze dropped to the black envelope in his hand, the white lettering stark against the matte surface.
‘It couldn’t be.’
‘No,’ Ashira echoed her thoughts.
Those envelopes were reserved for serious pack violations—official notices. Graham had no clue what he was holding. All he saw was a letter, branded with the seal of a powerful corporation, addressed to one of his lawyers.
“How did you get that?” she asked, doing her best to mask her rising panic.
“The mailroom supervisor had to sign for it. He flagged it due to the sending company,” he said with a shrug. “Standard protocol.”
Jaliyah stood, reaching for the envelope, but he pulled it back. “So again—how do you know them? Are they trying to recruit you?”
“No, they’re not,” she said quickly, shaking her head. “Can I have the envelope now?”
“Not until you explain,” he replied, voice flat and firm.
“Fine,” she sighed. “I grew up in the Wolfe Corporation. My family still works for them. I got kicked out when I turned 20.” She tried to swallow the ache that rose with the words. No matter how long it had been, she always missed home.
Graham’s light gray eyes locked on hers, reading her like a book. He was clearly trying to decide if she was telling the truth. He tapped the envelope again, then without warning, tore it open right in front of her.
Jaliyah silently begged the Goddess that the letter wasn’t written in Wolfen. Hopefully, the Alpha had the foresight to assume this could land in human hands.
She froze as he began reading aloud.
*****
Jaliyah Vale,
You have 3 days to respond to this letter.
You will return to Wolfe Corporation within 7 days.
Or I will have you brought in.
Zephyra Wolfe, CEO Wolfe Corporation
*****
Graham dumped the contents of the envelope into his palm. A long glass vial slid out, sealed with a cork. Inside was a single purple wolfsbane flower. It meant nothing to Graham. He studied it, frowning, turning the vial in his hand like it held some hidden clue.
But Jaliyah’s stomach dropped like a stone.
That flower was a warning. A threat from the new Alpha—her old friend, one-time lover. He wasn’t asking her to come back. He was demanding it. And if she didn’t comply, he’d force her return, whatever it took.
She hadn’t the slightest clue what he could want. The letter had no subject, no explanation—just a command to come home. Not that she wanted to. She’d left at his order, and she had no desire to go back. The Luna had despised her. Maybe now that he’d taken over, he and Soraya were finally ready to punish her—maybe even declare her rogue, in person.
Was he really that cruel? Would he go that far just to sever her from the pack?
Jaliyah snatched both the letter and the vial from Graham’s hand and read the note again. Ashira whimpered inside her, equally worried. If they went back, they couldn’t take the triplets. They’d have to find someone to care for them and hope—pray—that all this was about was her being cast out officially. If that was it, maybe she could come right back.
But the darker thoughts clawed at her.
What if the Luna wanted her tortured? Imprisoned? Or worse—dead? The idea of leaving her kids behind, possibly orphaned, shook her to her core. But she forced herself to shove the fear down.
No, Avery and Peyton could take them. They didn’t know anything about the wolf world, but they’d keep the children safe. Their first shift would scare the hell out of everyone, sure—but what choice did she have?
There was no way she could leave them with her own parents. Soraya would kill them the second she found out they were Zephyra’s. She’d never allow rival heirs to exist. And if they were sent to her family? Zephyra would smell them the second they entered the packlands—his wolf would know, instinctively. And Soraya? She wouldn’t waste a second getting rid of them.
Graham gently tapped her shoulder, pulling her back to reality. “What is this all about?”
“I don’t know,” she said honestly. “I’ve been gone six years, Graham. You hired me right out of law school. Haven’t I been here the whole time?”
He nodded slowly. “I don’t want to lose you, Jaliyah. Why not call the number at the bottom? Maybe you can land them as a client.”
‘Yeah, right.’ She nearly laughed. ‘Graham, you have no idea who he really is—or what he’s capable of.’
“I doubt I’d be able to,” she said honestly. “To tell you the truth, that man hates me.”
“Then why is he demanding you come back?”
“Maybe…” She paused, thinking. Aside from punishing her for attacking his Luna, there was only one other reason. The pack had funded her law degree. She was supposed to return and work in their legal department—be a functioning member of the pack.
“I think I owe them for law school,” she said. “Wolfe Corporation paid my tuition. I was meant to work for them after graduation. But I got kicked out halfway through and told never to come back—so I didn’t.”
“And they still paid your tuition?” Graham asked, clearly puzzled.
“Yeah. Thaddeus Wolfe was CEO at the time—Zephyra’s father. Maybe he thought I’d come back eventually.”
Graham nodded. “Do you have the money to pay them back?”
Jaliyah sighed. “Not the full amount. Maybe half.” If that was all they wanted—just reimbursement—she could handle it. She could even write up the repayment contract herself, with bulletproof clauses. She’d make sure he left her alone once it was paid. Maybe even add a clause saying she’d transfer to another pack afterward, cutting all ties.
The real question was—could she do all this without Zephyra discovering the children? He wouldn’t suspect they were his—unless he saw them in person. But even then, could she find a pack that wouldn’t use the kids as leverage once they realized who their father was?
Too many unknowns.
“I could write you a contract, give you the rest of the money,” Graham offered. “You can pay me back when you’re able.”
Jaliyah gave him a small, grateful smile. She knew why he was offering. Her last divorce case had brought the firm five million in profit. The client had been so thrilled, he referred his sister for a prenup. Jaliyah was gold to this firm—sharp, professional, relentless. She never overlooked a detail, never backed down, never left a case unfinished. Someone had once called her a dog with a bone. They had no idea how true that was.
“No need,” she said. “Once the settlement from my last case hits and you pay me, I’ll have the money.”
Graham looked pleased. “I’ll get that processed ASAP.”
“I’d really appreciate that,” she said, watching him leave her office.
She dropped into her leather chair, thankful for the comfort. The $2,500 price tag had been worth it. Resting her head on the desk, she whispered, “Three days.”
She could run. Three days was enough time to sever her pack ties and disappear. But Ashira chimed in, “The second we do, he’ll know. He’ll come after us—angrier than ever.”
“I know,” Jaliyah replied. “But maybe… maybe he won’t care. Maybe he’ll just let us go. What else can we do?”
Ashira huffed. She needed to think too. Between the two of them, surely they could come up with a plan.
Or maybe… maybe they had just three days to build up the courage to make a call Jaliyah never wanted to make. To hear his voice again—cold, angry, full of hatred for the woman who had dared to harm his Mate… now his Luna.
There would be no warmth. No flirtation. No sultry teasing like there’d once been, when he used to whisper dirty promises into her ear during nights full of pleasure. Nights she couldn’t forget, no matter how hard she tried. Nights that haunted her dreams, especially during the full moon.
Even though she and Ashira had let him go, they would always be bonded to him—through the children he didn’t even know existed. The only pieces of their old life that remained.
Liam was no comparison in bed—not to him. But how could he be? Liam was human.
She let out a tired sigh, eyes closing.
‘Three days...’

Chapter 5
Zephyra
That woman was absolutely infuriating. Today was the deadline—the third day since her company had signed for the letter. Why hadn’t she called yet? Was she really that dumb to think he wouldn’t follow through? It was getting late. He knew there was a three-hour time difference, so he had to give her until 5 p.m. her time, which meant 8 p.m. for him. Zephyra checked his watch—it was already a quarter to eight. She wasn’t going to call. She was going to make him act.
Darian leaned casually against the wall next to the desk, his usual spot, watching Zephyra pace behind it.
“She’ll call,” he said simply, like he could read Zephyra’s mind. “It’s Jaliyah.”
“Time’s almost up,” Zephyra snapped. If she didn’t call, he’d have no choice but to follow through—even if he didn’t want to. Ember, his wolf, was already pissed at him because of the official letter and the threat it carried. She wasn’t even talking to him because of it. Lately, she’d been acting... different.
His frustration over Jaliyah’s silence was boiling into full-blown anger. Even though Ember wasn’t speaking, she was pacing inside his head, restless. Zephyra was starting to believe she had no intention of calling. She had a new life now—away from the pack, away from them, away from him. If he was being totally honest, part of him had expected her to cut ties completely.
To bolt. To make him hunt her down. And he would’ve. Ember loved a good chase, and Jaliyah had been his favorite pursuit once upon a time. But she hadn’t run... yet. That didn’t mean she wouldn’t in the next ten minutes.
The door to his office opened and in walked his father, Thaddeus. He took in the scene—Zephyra pacing, Darian watching—and sighed.
“What’s going on, son?”
“Jaliyah. I gave her three days to call, and seven to come back.” His tone was sharp. He didn’t feel like explaining himself—didn’t need to. He’d been Alpha for two years now. The comment was just a courtesy, out of respect for his father as the former Alpha.
“You didn’t send the black envelope, did you?” Thaddeus’s voice was edged with disappointment.
“Yes.” That was all Zephyra said. He watched his father’s icy blue eyes swing to Darian, looking for confirmation—like he thought Zephyra might be lying. When Darian nodded, Thaddeus’s anger flared.
“Why in the name of the Moon Goddess would you do that?” He ran both hands through his hair, pulling at it in frustration.
Zephyra felt like he owed him an explanation now. “She wouldn’t come home when I asked nicely. Ignored all the requests—three of them! HOW DARE SHE!” He shouted the last part, unable to contain it. He was the Alpha of the Moonhowl Tribe. She was still part of this pack. His pack. That meant she was under his command. And she had the audacity to ignore him. No—she defied him. Even after he’d extended an olive branch and told her to come home.
His fists clenched, and he slammed one down on the corner of the desk, the wood cracking under the impact. She used to never say no to him. It had always been “yes,” always followed by a sweet smile and a teasing wink.
But not anymore. She had changed. And his rage was ready to erupt. One glance at the clock—two minutes left.
Darian’s phone rang just as Zephyra was mentally willing his office phone to ring instead. ‘Come on, ring.’ But it was Darian’s phone that broke the silence, and that pushed Zephyra over the edge. How dare someone interrupt him right now?
He heard Darian answer in that laid-back tone Zephyra hated, “Hello, Beta Darian speaking.”
Zephyra’s fury exploded. “Send the worst of the worst. Drag her ass back here!” he roared, slamming both fists on the desk. The wood cracked again. He didn’t care.
Darian stopped mid-sentence and stared at him. He could feel his father’s gaze, too. Darian looked back at his phone, sighed deeply, and then leveled a hard stare at him—one that felt like a challenge.
“Well, Alpha, that went well,” Darian said flatly. Then he dropped the bomb. “That was Jaliyah. She heard everything you just said... and hung up. All I got was a gasp—scared as hell.”
Zephyra ran his hands through his hair in frustration, pulling hard. Damn it, he was turning into his father. He shut his eyes.
“Call her back. Now,” he ordered, trying not to kick something across the room.
Ember was growling inside him. ‘Look what you did.’
‘I know,’ Zephyra replied. ‘I’ll fix it.’
‘You’d better,’ he snapped back.
Zephyra watched as Darian hit redial. Then he noticed the name on Darian's screen: Jaliyah. That son of a bitch had her number all along. Zephyra was going to punch him in the face as soon as this mess was over. They could’ve just called her earlier, and he wouldn’t have lost it like that.
Why the hell did she wait until the last damn minute? He wasn’t exactly known for his patience these days. His father was still standing there, waiting, but more interested in Zephyra’s reaction than the actual outcome. He was leaning against the doorframe, eyebrow raised, curiosity written all over his face.
Zephyra glared at him. “What?”
“Son, you seem real bent outta shape over one little she-wolf. The same one you ordered away years ago... What’s really going on here? Why are you so desperate to bring her back now?”
‘That’s my business,’ Zephyra thought. He could do what he wanted. But he knew his father wouldn’t let it go. As the former Alpha, he still had the right to ask—and get an answer. He remained in charge when Zephyra was handling business, at Council meetings, or helping allied packs under threat.
Zephyra turned back to Darian.
“She didn’t answer.”
Darian was already redialing. “That’s weird... the line’s not connecting now,” he said, frowning at his phone.
“Just freaking great,” Zephyra snapped, the anger rising again—this time at himself. He knew he was the reason she wasn’t picking up. She heard him yell and panicked. ‘She’s probably running now.’
Ember sounded pissed. ‘Brilliant move, dumbass.’
Zephyra didn’t even argue. He agreed.
“Darian, make arrangements. Who do you know out there?”
“A couple wolves. They’re not retrieval specialists, but money talks.”
“Then pay them. She’s running. We need to move fast.” Zephyra nodded.
His father let out a deep sigh, drawing his attention.
“I’d go myself, son. That’d be better.”
“She’ll be long gone before I—or anyone else—gets there,” Zephyra said, and it was true. Even with his private jet, it would take too long.
“Hmm. Still…” Thaddeus didn’t seem as worried as he should be.
Zephyra brushed it off. Who knew what his dad thought anymore? Retirement had mellowed him out. He was more relaxed about everything these days. When Zephyra had asked him about it last year, Thaddeus had just shrugged and said, “You’ve got the stress now, son. I get to spend time with my Mate. A lot of time,” grinning like a teenager. “If you know what I mean.”
Oh, Zephyra knew. The whole pack knew. His parents had basically reverted to horny teens. With them no longer in charge, they spent most of their time... mating. In the woods, in the house, in wolf form or human—it didn’t matter. Half the pack had seen them going at it, especially during full moons.
Zephyra watched as his father walked out of the office.
“I wonder where my pretty girl is right now,” Thaddeus murmured, heading off to find her.
Zephyra prayed she was in their room. The last thing he wanted was to walk in on them somewhere in the pack house again. He shook his head.
They really had turned back the clock.

Chapter 6
Jaliyah
It had taken every ounce of courage she had to make the call. She’d already decided—she wasn’t dialing the packhouse. No way. She couldn’t face talking to him right now. Instead, she punched in Beta Darian’s number. It had been six long years, and she could still picture the fury in his eyes, feel the force of the command he'd hit her with. Her chest ached at the memory, and she rubbed it without thinking, trying to ease the sting.
She’d spent the whole day staring at that number. It was nearly 5 PM now. The deadline was closing in. Thankfully, Avery and Peyton had agreed to take the triplets for a few days while she went away on a “business trip.” ‘Thank the Goddess for them,’ she thought silently, sending a prayer of gratitude. Human or not, they were blessings—gifts from the Moon Goddess as far as she was concerned.
Sitting in her office chair, she finally dialed the number listed at the bottom of the letter. Darian’s voice came through the line—smooth, gentle, almost purring. Calm and composed, like nothing ever rattled him. But she knew better. She’d grown up with him. That calm was just a mask.
The rage she’d heard in Alpha Zephyra’s voice when he gave that order—she never thought he’d be capable of directing that kind of hatred at her. “Send the worst of the worst.” That command had sent a chill straight down to her soul.
Ashira, her wolf, whimpered in response. A sharp gasp escaped her lips, and without thinking, she ended the call. She stared, horrified, at her phone, every part of her screaming to run—now—and never look back. Ashira didn’t argue.
He was still so furious. So full of rage. It felt like he didn’t just hate her—he despised her. How could he? After everything they’d been through? A lifetime of friendship, of love—erased with one slap? That was all it took for him to throw it all away. In the end, only his Luna mattered to him. Not their bond. Not their past.
Her phone started ringing again. Darian. She saw the number and hit decline. She stood up, fists clenched. She meant nothing to him now. Nothing. With a snarl, she slammed her fist down on the phone, shattering it into pieces, shards flying in every direction.
“Time to go,” she muttered under her breath. She grabbed her briefcase and headed home.
She’d tell the triplets they were going on vacation, then catch the first international flight out. They all had passports, had traveled before. Singapore sounded good—wolves were practically nonexistent there. That could work. But this time, she needed to choose somewhere more suitable for Ashira.
City life had been hard on her wolf. Ashira barely got to shift, thanks to the need to stay hidden from the Wolfen world. And rogue territory? Absolutely not. Way too risky. No matter how fast Ashira was, it wasn’t worth the danger. If something went wrong, their pups would be orphaned in the human world.
The drive home from the office took over an hour now that she’d moved so far out. Rush hour traffic didn’t help. The only thing working in her favor was that she was on the other side of the country from him. That gave her a window—10 to 12 hours maybe. He’d need to arrange flights and transportation for his men.
She’d be long gone by then. This was it. No turning back. She’d sever her last ties with the pack once at the airport. Too many scents to track there. And once she went rogue, her pack scent would fade. Even now, he could still track her by it.
“It’s going to hurt us.”
“I know. But what choice do we have? ‘The worst of the worst,’ Ashira. That means whoever he sends can do whatever they want... and no one will stop them.”
Ashira shuddered in disgust. “I’ll kill anyone who touches us, Jaliyah.”
“I know we’ll try. But...” They both knew they’d be outnumbered. She’d trained all her life, sure—still trained weekly. But these men? They’d be twice her size, trained daily, and probably took pleasure in hurting people. Fighting back would only rile them up.
She parked in front of her building instead of the secure garage. She didn’t plan to stay long—just enough time to pack suitcases and grab passports. An hour tops. Hopefully less.
She stepped out of the car, mind racing about where to go. Once she was rogue, there was no going back. So somewhere with no wolves made the most sense. A country with no natural wolf population. Other shifters wouldn’t bother her if she wasn’t a threat.
Somewhere small. Secluded. Somewhere with forests for Ashira—and eventually, for her kids, once they could shift and run free. She had a degree in contract law, which was always in demand. If not that, she could do translation work—she spoke three languages. That gave her options.
The cloth pressed to her mouth came out of nowhere—just like the steel grip around her waist that yanked her backward into a solid chest. She hadn’t seen, heard, or smelled anything out of place. She’d been too deep in her thoughts.
She gasped in shock—an inhale that sucked the chloroform deep into her lungs. Her vision blurred almost instantly. Ashira snarled in her mind, claws bursting from Jaliyah’s fingertips, ready to fight. But then came a sharp sting in her neck—something injected—and a searing pain spread through her veins like fire.
“No—” she tried to scream, but the darkness was already closing in. Her last thought before it took her completely: ‘My babies... I’m sorry.’
*****
Her eyelids felt like they weighed a ton. She was so tired. Just opening her eyes was a struggle. Minutes passed before she could keep them open long enough to see.
She was lying on her right side, barely able to move. Her arms were tied behind her. ‘Ashira,’ she called out in her mind. Nothing. She couldn’t feel her at all. Not even a trace.
They’d used wolfsbane. She was completely cut off from her wolf. The burning on her wrists told her the cuffs were silver. She was as helpless as a human now.
She breathed in slowly, trying to assess. She was in the back of a moving van, still in her clothes. No pain between her legs—thank the Goddess. Not that she’d want to be awake for that kind of violation, but still... she had no idea how long she’d been out. Hours? A full day?
The kids had been with their nanny. How long before she noticed something was wrong? Would she call the police? Stay with the triplets? She had to believe Suzzy would protect them. They paid her well, treated her with kindness. She loved those kids. She’d stay.
Jaliyah forced herself to stay calm. It was the only way she’d survive this and find a chance to escape.
It was midweek. If she didn’t return home or show up at work, someone would report her missing. Human cops couldn’t do much in the Wolfen world, but the packs still had to play nice occasionally.
A boot nudged her chest, rolling her onto her back.
“Well, look who’s awake,” came a gravelly male voice, laced with amusement. “What’d you do, I wonder?” He chuckled.
Jaliyah stared up at him. It was dark inside the van—she couldn’t tell if it was nighttime, or if the van was blacked out to avoid being seen. She was only wearing a blouse and skirt—easy to rip off. Her only weapons now were her mind and a pair of stilettos.
“Please,” she whispered. “I have children.”
She hoped he had a heart. Wolves were fiercely protective of their young. Maybe she could appeal to that.
“Three kids. Please, let me go.”
He looked at her for a long moment, then shrugged. “Already been paid.” His voice was suddenly cold, detached—like he had to shut off all emotion to do this.
“They’re only five. No father.” Her voice cracked. She was begging now.
He frowned again, stared at her. He looked conflicted—for a moment, she thought it might be working. Then another shrug. “Not my problem, lady.”
Jaliyah pushed herself to a seated position. He just watched her—wary, but not worried. She looked harmless. No wolf. Hands cuffed in silver. But what he didn’t know was that her father had been a top warrior.
He’d trained her from the time she was five. Every day, with and without her wolf. He always said she needed to be ready. That one day, someone would come for her.
This was that day.
She thought of everything her father had drilled into her—fight, never give up, ignore the pain. Use anything—wit, charm, seduction, even a splinter of wood. Just throw them off for a second. That’s all you need.
The van slowed down. The man glanced away for just a moment. That was her chance.
She pushed herself to her knees, then used the van wall to get to her feet. As soon as he looked back, she launched herself off the wall, slamming into him with everything she had. Just like Dad taught her.
His head smacked the opposite wall with a sickening crack. She heard it. Probably a concussion. His wolf growled, and she scrambled to get away, pulling herself upright.
But she lost her footing and fell backward.
He shot up fast, yelling, “What the fuck!” as he reached for her. She kicked out with both feet, and one of her stiletto heels drove straight into his gut with a sickening, wet sound. She could feel the warm rush of his blood soaking her foot almost instantly. His agonized scream told her she’d hit deep. Thank the Goddess she always wore four-inch heels.
Her heel tore free from his body, blood pouring down his shirt. The van jerked to a sudden stop as he lunged for her again, but the motion threw him off balance and he fell. Jaliyah yanked her knee up to block his weight as he collapsed on top of her. She gasped under the pressure—he was heavy.
“Bitch, look what you did to me!” he snarled, pushing himself up and grabbing her with both hands, his wolf strength surging as he hauled her off the floor by her waist.
“What the hell happened?” came another man’s voice from the front of the van.
“She-wolf fucking attacked me,” he snapped, pain in his voice. He spun her around so her back was to him—clearly not risking another strike.
Jaliyah felt the sticky wetness of his blood on her blouse, soaking through the back. The warm slickness seeped down into her shoe, pooling at the ball of her foot. The metallic scent of blood was overwhelming now that he had her pinned to him. His wound hadn’t healed yet, though she knew it wouldn’t be long before his wolf started to mend it.
His grip was tighter now—tense, cautious. The side door of the van slid open, and a new man appeared. Tall, lean, all muscle. He wore plain clothes—blue jeans, a basic blue tee. His dark brown eyes took in the scene, his wolf right at the surface, ready to act. Jaliyah could see the faint green glow behind his irises—it would take over if she acted out.
She wasn’t that big—five-seven, lean but strong—and probably looked small and fragile to him right now. She watched him carefully, trying to calculate how much danger she was in. She made herself look vulnerable, helpless.
Apparently, his wolf didn’t think much of her—it retreated, leaving the man in charge. A grin tugged at his lips.
“Come on, pretty thing. We’re almost there. Be good now.”
Jaliyah pressed herself harder against the wolf holding her, as if his touch disgusted her.
“Don’t touch me,” she hissed, already bracing to strike.
“Aw, come on. You’re too pretty to ruin,” he said, leaning into the van to grab her.
Jaliyah lashed out, her right foot shooting up. He didn’t see it coming. Her heel slammed into his neck, right where she aimed. His eyes went wide in shock as he jerked back, her heel ripping free. Blood sprayed from his neck as he clutched it, life slipping away fast. She’d nailed his carotid artery. Nothing but a miracle from the Goddess could save him now.
The man holding her cursed violently, so loud it made her ears ring. Then, without warning, he shoved her out of the van.
She hit the gravel face-first, unable to catch herself. Her cheek scraped the ground from temple to chin, pain exploding through her face. Her shoulder slammed down, then her hip, her chest screaming as she slid across the rough road. The agony stole her breath. Tears streamed from her eyes as she lay there, too hurt to move.
Not that she had time.
A hand grabbed her by the hair and yanked her off the ground. She screamed, sure her scalp was about to be torn off. Then her back hit the van hard. Two hands wrapped around her throat, lifting her off the ground, choking the life from her.
A third man had shown up—this one meant to kill her.
“That was my brother, you bitch! I’ll kill you!” he screamed, spit flying into her face.
Jaliyah had no way to defend herself. Her hands were still cuffed behind her, bound in silver. His body blocked her legs from doing any real damage. She couldn’t breathe. Her lungs burned from the earlier fall, and now she was being strangled to death.
Suddenly, he was gone.
She crumpled to the ground, too weak to stand. Her knees gave out beneath her. Nearby, a fight had broken out. She could hear it—growling, shouting. She struggled to stay conscious.
“I told you—no harm to her!” one man shouted.
“She killed my brother!” the other roared.
Jaliyah leaned against the van, finally sucking in a full breath. She looked toward the ground. The man she’d attacked was dead. The one who’d been in the van with her was cradling his lifeless body.
She didn’t care.
They’d drugged her. Kidnapped her. Left her babies alone and unprotected.
Drawing in another shaky breath, she took her chance.
Everyone was distracted.
She turned and ran—down the road, away from the wolves, away from the van.
Surely someone would stop if they saw her—bloody, beaten, bound. No human would ignore a woman in this state.
But just minutes later, she was slammed into the ground again. Pain shot through her body as fresh injuries layered onto the old. Her knees screamed in protest.
Two wolves lifted her to her feet and started dragging her back. She tried to fight, but the pain was too much.
They were stronger. Bigger. They didn’t stop.
As she looked up the road, horror sank into her bones.
She was home.
The big black gates of the Moonhowl Tribe stood ahead. The van had stopped about 300 meters out, likely from her earlier scuffle. One gate was open, the other still closed, but she recognized the red circle painted on the shut half—the symbol of the Blood Moon. What the pack was named for.
She fought harder, panic surging in her chest, but it was useless. They just tightened their grip and kept pushing forward.
She could see the car waiting beyond the gate. Its back door stood open.
Behind her, the sounds of fighting had stopped.
Tears streamed down her face—pain, fear, and the dread of what was coming.
If this was just the beginning, what more was in store?
A sob escaped her. She knew who was waiting. Her heart ached at the thought.
Would she ever see her children again?
A hand touched her left elbow. The wolves let go instantly.
“Nice to see you again, Jaliyah,” came a soft, familiar voice—Beta Darian.
“I’ll take her from here, boys.”
He led her toward the gate and the car. She didn’t resist. Once, they’d been close friends. Not anymore. But she knew she couldn’t fight him. There were only a few in the Moonhowl Tribe who could take Darian one-on-one—and she wasn’t one of them.
Her face throbbed. Her knees barely held her up. She was covered in blood and wounds. And she had no Ashira to heal her. No one to ease the pain.
She just had to endure it.
She could feel Darian’s eyes on her but kept hers down. What could she say to make him let her go? To betray his Alpha—his best friend?
Nothing.
So she said nothing. Just let the silent tears fall down her ruined face. She probably looked as miserable as she felt.
He sighed as they reached the car. He helped her inside, then slid in beside her.
“Straight to the packhouse,” he told the driver.
Her fate was sealed now.
All she could do was pray to the Goddess to protect her babies. She sent up the prayer with every ounce of love she had left in her.

title: That knot in your shoulder blade isn’t a muscle problem.
body:
Most doctors miss this when people have that deep, stubborn knot at the inner edge of their shoulder blade that never fully goes away.

You know the one. That spot that feels like a nail being pressed into your back. The one you reach back and press on constantly without even realizing you're doing it. The one that gets worse as the day goes on, sometimes sends numbness down your arm, and never — no matter what you try — actually releases.

I spent two years being told different things about it.

Sleeping position. Muscle tension from stress. Rhomboid strain. Sit up straighter. Stretch more.

I tried everything I was told. Massage every few weeks — it felt incredible for a day and then the nail was back. Tennis ball against the wall, digging into that exact spot until it went numb. Heating pad every evening. A theragun attachment my husband bought that helped for about forty minutes.

Nothing touched it. Not for more than a day. And all of them where almost painful

And the frustrating part wasn't just the pain. It was that I'd been rubbing and pressing and treating the same spot for two years and it kept coming back in the exact same place. Like something was putting it there.

Turns out something was.

I finally went to a physical therapist who specialized in cervical spine issues. Not a general physio — someone who specifically worked with nerve and spine conditions. I wasn't expecting anything new. I'd been told the same things enough times that I'd mostly accepted this was just how my upper back worked now.

She watched me move for a few minutes, pressed on a few spots in my neck, and then pulled up an image on her screen.

It was a diagram of the cervical spine — the vertebrae in your neck — with nerves branching out from between each one like roots from a tree.

"These nerves don't just stay in your neck," she said. "They travel. This one here branches out and runs along the inner edge of your shoulder blade all the way down your arm. When a disc in your neck shifts and presses on this nerve, the pain shows up wherever that nerve goes."

She pointed to my shoulder blade.

"That knot you keep pressing on isn't a muscle problem. It's where that nerve ends up."

I sat there for a second trying to process that.

Two years of treating my shoulder blade. The problem was in my neck the whole time.

She explained that when a disc in the cervical spine compresses a nerve root, the muscles along that nerve's pathway tighten up to protect the area. That's the knot. That's why it feels like something solid under the skin. And that's why massage, lacrosse balls, and stretching never fix it — because you're working on the muscle that's reacting, not the compressed nerve causing the reaction.

"Every time you dig into that spot, you're getting temporary relief because you're releasing the muscle briefly. But the disc is still pressing on the nerve. So the muscle gets the signal to tighten right back up."

That explained everything. The massage that wore off by the time I got home. The lacrosse ball that helped for an hour. The stretches that felt good for five minutes and then the nail was back.

She said what actually fixes it is cervical decompression — specific traction at a 26-degree angle that creates space between the vertebrae and takes the pressure off the nerve root directly. Combined with heat to release the muscles that have been chronically tight along that nerve pathway. And targeted vibration to break up the deep tension that had been building for years, the kind that surface treatments never reach because it sits too far underneath.

That's what spine clinics use. Sessions run $80 to $150. Two to three times a week. Most people try it for a few weeks, can't keep up with the cost, stop — and the knot comes right back because the compression was never fully resolved.

She mentioned that a group of physical therapists and cervical spine engineers had looked at exactly that problem and built something people could use at home. Same 26-degree angle, same heat, same vibration — in a single device, fifteen minutes a day, without the appointments.

I ordered it that night. I told myself not to expect anything because I'd been let down enough times to know better.

The first week I still caught myself reaching back to press on that spot out of habit. But the nail — that constant deep pressure — wasn't hitting the same intensity by the afternoon.

Week two I was sitting at my desk and realized I'd gone most of the morning without thinking about my shoulder blade. Then I reached across the table for something and noticed my arm felt normal. No tingling. No that-feeling-is-coming warning.

I sat there for a second waiting for it to catch up with me.

It didn't.

That was the first time I actually believed something had changed.

A few weeks later a friend asked if I'd done something different. I'd stopped doing the lacrosse ball routine and the evening heating pad and she'd noticed I seemed less distracted. Less somewhere else.

If you have that same knot — the one that's always in the same spot, that massage never fixes, that comes back every single time — it might not be a shoulder problem at all.

It might be a nerve in your neck that nobody has checked.

The device is called FisioRest. It's what she recommended. It's what I used. It's the first thing that addressed what was actually causing that knot instead of just working on where I felt it.

If you see yourself anywhere in this, there's a link below.

The knot isn't in your shoulder blade. It never was.

But my father called me opportunity.
He bartered me 
for ten million dollars.
That was the beginning of my doom. 
Alpha Edward didn’t see a child. He saw a mine. "
He burned my palms with hot iron rods,
trying to force gold from my skin.
Something white sparks before he could break me.
And the Moon Goddess descended,
“I am taking the child’s blessing, when she turns eighteen, she will take everything from you.”
A golden light tore from my hands 
and vanished into the sky.
My power disappeared. But my suffering didn’t.
Alpha Edward grew afraid.
So he handed me to his daughter.
“Make her your slave. Suppress her before she outshines you.”
Marcy obeyed. She didn’t kill me. She ended me slowly.
Years of hunger.
Bruises.
Chains.
Servitude. "

There were whispers through the pack. Electric, hushed, breathless. A visitor was coming.
Alpha Damon.

Leader of the Dark Howlers, fiercest pack in the realm. He was the most powerful Alpha in all of North America. Women threw themselves at him. Rulers feared him. He could seduce a she-wolf with a glance, or tear out a man’s throat just as easily.
Damon was untouchable. 
He scorned the idea of love. Rejected every political match. Not a single potential bride, despite the many presented, could win his affection. None were worthy of being his Luna, the proud she-wolf to rule by his side.
Love was a distraction, an attempt to tame him. And Damon would never be tamed. 
Still, there were those who tried. 

Alpha Edward, leader of the Red Moon pack, was desperate to secure his political power. He invited Damon to meet his daughter, Princess Marcy, beautiful, cunning, cruel. She intended to make him hers.
Talia feared their union. Would Marcy succeed where so many others had failed? Would Marcy’s cruelty only intensify as Luna to such a powerful Alpha? 

The moment Alpha Damon stepped onto Red Moon Pack grounds with his mated Betas, Caden and Maya, something felt off. His wolf stirred uneasily beneath the surface. Damon didn’t need confirmation, he already knew: no one in the Red Moon Pack could be trusted.

They all sat down in the dining hall, its gaudy opulence a reflection of Red Moon’s inflated ego.

Marcy arrived fashionably late, every detail of her appearance sharpened like a blade. Shimmering blond hair, a sculpted figure. She was the type of girl who got what she wanted.
Her friend, Nora, wasn’t as restrained. She eyed Damon with hunger, her gaze sliding over him like a caress. The rumors had reached her ears: about his appetite, his stamina, his size. She didn’t care that Marcy was supposed to win the Alpha’s hand. Nora wanted a taste for herself.
Marcy’s mother, Luna Layla, noticed the heat in Nora’s stare… and the flicker of fury in her daughter’s eyes.
“Marcy,” Layla said, too sweetly, “Why don’t you show Alpha Damon to his room so you two can… talk?”

While the Red Moon Pack celebrated Damon’s arrival, elsewhere in the kitchens, Talia worked until the sweat stung her eyes. All she could dream of was the scraps she might scavenge when the feast was over.
The other Omegas had different plans for her.
Anna, their cruel ringleader, stepped into Talia’s path, towering over her, “Listen up, slave.” The other Omegas giggled behind her like hyenas. 
Anna’s lips twisted into a cruel smirk. “You’re going to deliver towels to Alpha Damon’s room.”
Talia froze. “Right now? But... what if he’s inside?”
Anna raised her hand, ready to strike. “Are you questioning me?”
Talia flinched, her heart pounding. Without her wolf, she was defenseless against the bullies. 
Without another word, she took the towels and hurried off, every step dragging her closer to the Alpha’s quarters and whatever fate awaited her behind that door.

When Talia entered the room, she froze. Damon was in his room. But he wasn’t alone. 
There was Marcy. On her knees. Between Damon’s legs. 
Marcy whipped around, her eyes blazing with fury as they locked onto Talia’s. The insolence! 
A jolt of fear shot up Talia’s spine. Retribution would be certain.
Damon’s eyes snapped to Talia.
“Stop!” he barked.
But Talia was gone, bolting from the room, too terrified to look back.
What Talia didn’t know, what she couldn’t have known, is that in that moment, Damon’s world had shifted.
Her scent. It hit his veins like a spark of kindling, igniting something primal within him.
Could it be? His inner wolf howled the truth within him, again and again. She, a lowly omega, a serving girl without a friend, was his fated mate?

Ignoring the mocking laughter of Anna and the others, Talia ran until she reached the attic, shoving the cabinet against the door before collapsing in the corner, struggling to quiet her frantic breathing.
'Is this it? Is this the day I die?'

Back in Damon’s room, Marcy landed clumsily on her backside as Damon shoved her away, his expression thunderous and unreadable.
"Who was that girl?" he demanded, hastily buttoning his pants.
Marcy knew exactly who she was. Talia. That wolf-less bitch. How dare she step into an Alpha’s chambers uninvited? And worse, if word got out that Marcy had been pleasuring Damon before he’d even proposed... she’d be humiliated. A laughingstock. Her reputation would be in shreds.
Marcy’s jaw clenched with fury. She should’ve done more than just beat the girl this morning.
But Damon didn’t notice Marcy’s simmering rage. He was too distracted, his mind replaying the moment when she walked in. How that intoxicating scent, freesia and citrus, had struck him. How his wolf had howled, wild and urgent. All he could think about was pulling her into his arms.
'Mate.' His wolf howled.  In confirmation, I couldnt my wolf had been silenced years ago. 

My name is Talia, but no one calls me Talia except for teachers on the first day of schooling. I'm more popular as the wolfless freak. I'm a werewolf in the red moon pack. Since I'm an orphan, I'm not completely sure how old I am, but I'm pretty sure I'm 16. Also, I'm an omega, which means I'm a servant. My job is to make the meals for the werewolves who live in the pack house. Between making breakfast and dinner for over 100 wolves, cleaning up after them, and restocking the pantries of the ranked members' apartments on the 3rd and 4th floors, I do normal teenager stuff, except I don't have a lot of spare time to do so. Homework is the extent of living my teen life. Right now it's 11:30 at night. I'm putting the finishing touches on my English essay when I hear the door of the dungeon slam open. Great. Now what did I do? It doesn't take much. 
Alpha Edward is an alcoholic. It's really difficult for werewolves to get drunk, which means you have to drink heavily to feel the effects. This means he probably had a fight with Luna Layla about his drinking. Which means she locked him out of their room. Which means he has come down to take out his anger on me. Just an average Tuesday in the packhouse. I know the drill. I'm already on my feet waiting for him. I'm thinking in my mind. “Alpha Edward, what can I do for you?" I ask with my eyes looking at the floor. I keep my hands clasped in front of me, trying to look as small as possible. Without a word, a whiskey bottle whizzes past my ear and smashes against the wall above my cot. I flinch and can't help but start to tremble and hug myself.
